newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin "probably knew" of sauna scandal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin "probably knew" of sauna scandal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin suspended his justice minister on Wednesday pending investigation of a film purporting to show him with naked women in a gangland sauna.
A Kremlin spokesman said Yeltsin had probably known of the scandal surrounding minister Valentin Kovalyov before it broke last week. "I think he knew about it beforehand," he told Reuters.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov was earlier quoted as confirming the film in question was genuine and saying he told Yeltsin of it as early as April.
However, the spokesman said he believed Yeltsin had probably ordered the probe into the allegations only after he returned on Monday from a Group of Seven summit in the United States.

Yeltsin's decree said Kovalyov was suspended "in connection with the need to carry out an investigation into media publications which discredit the minister". There was no indication of how long that would take.
Kovalyov, 53, has suggested the video was faked. He himself had asked to be suspended to give him time to clear his name.
Colleagues of the ex-communist justice minister in the liberal-dominated government were reported on Tuesday to have urged Yeltsin to sack him outright.

The monthly newspaper Sovershenno Sekretno (Top Secret) last week published grainy snaps taken from a video which it said showed Kovalyov in the sauna of a Moscow gangland nightclub in September 1995. He took office in January that year.
Russian television stations later aired the video.

Yet the scandal, all but unprecedented in Russia, has failed to stir great interest among the public or even the racier sections of the press, which have devoted most space to theories of a Byzantine criminal plot rather than Kovalyov's behaviour.
Several politicians have leapt to the minister's defence, saying what he does in his spare time is his own business.
Kulikov was quoted by Interfax as saying there were at least five copies of the tape, which was seized by police this year when they arrested a banker charged with stealing $7 million.
On Monday, Kulikov said the publication of the Kovalyov film was an attempt by the banker's friends to discredit the police and wreck the case against him.

Chief prosecutor Yuri Skuratov repeated on Wednesday that criminal cases could be based on various grounds, including faking the film, invasion of privacy and breaching confidentiality of evidence in a police investigation.
In an interview in the Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper, Skuratov also speculated on the motives for the film's release. "This doesn't make the interior ministry look good," he said.
